pharm: Long-acting nondepolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant that competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at the motor end-plate nicotinic receptors, producing skeletal muscle paralysis; used as an adjunct to general anesthesia and for ventilated patients.
quick: Intubation: 0.06-0.1 mg/kg IV; maintenance 0.01-0.02 mg/kg IV as needed
Use only if clearly needed; quaternary agent crosses placenta minimally; can be used at cesarean section by anesthesia specialists
Single perioperative use; not expected to be significant in milk
Reduce dose / expect prolonged block - significant renal excretion; accumulation in renal failure
Prolonged onset and duration; reduced clearance - titrate carefully
Peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four), ventilation, BP/HR; ALWAYS ventilate
summary: Pancuronium is a long-acting nondepolarizing (aminosteroid) neuromuscular blocking agent used as an adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation, provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery, and aid controlled ventilation in critically ill patients. It competitively blocks acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors of the motor end-plate, causing flaccid paralysis. CRITICAL: pancuronium produces NO sedation, analgesia, or amnesia - patients must receive adequate anesthesia/sedation and analgesia, and ventilation MUST be controlled because respiratory muscles are paralyzed. It should be given only by clinicians experienced in airway management with facilities for intubation and mechanical ventilation immediately available. The usual intubating dose is 0.06-0.1 mg/kg IV. It has vagolytic and mild sympathomimetic effects that can raise heart rate and blood pressure. Block is reversed with an anticholinesterase (neostigmine) plus an antimuscarinic, or by sugammadex where available.
indications: Adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation
Facilitation of controlled mechanical ventilation in intensive care / critically ill patients

dosage.d: 0.06-0.1 mg/kg IV (initial); under balanced anesthesia an intubating dose around 0.06-0.08 mg/kg
dosage.t: Single bolus; onset ~2-3 min, intubating conditions ~3-5 min
dosage.n: Give only with airway and ventilation support ready

dosage.d: 0.01-0.02 mg/kg IV incremental doses as needed
dosage.t: Every ~25-60 min as guided by nerve stimulator

dosage.d: Intermittent boluses titrated to nerve-stimulator monitoring; reduce in renal/hepatic impairment
dosage.n: Ensure ongoing sedation and analgesia; avoid accumulation

admin: Administer intravenously only, by or under the supervision of clinicians experienced in neuromuscular blockade and airway management
Facilities for endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, oxygen, and reversal agents must be immediately available
Ensure adequate general anesthesia/sedation and analgesia - pancuronium provides paralysis only, with no effect on consciousness or pain
Monitor depth of block with a peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four)
Reverse residual block with an anticholinesterase (e.g., neostigmine) plus an antimuscarinic agent when spontaneous recovery has begun, or with sugammadex if available
moa: Pancuronium is a bisquaternary aminosteroid nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker. It competes with acetylcholine for the nicotinic cholinergic receptors at the motor end-plate of skeletal muscle, binding the receptor without activating it and thereby preventing depolarization and muscle contraction. The result is dose-dependent skeletal muscle relaxation progressing to flaccid paralysis. Because the block is competitive, it can be antagonized by increasing acetylcholine at the junction with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (neostigmine), or reversed by encapsulation with sugammadex. Pancuronium also has vagolytic (antimuscarinic) activity and can cause some catecholamine release, often producing a rise in heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to pancuronium or to the bromide ion
Use outside settings with airway control and mechanical ventilation capability
relative: Myasthenia gravis and myasthenic (Eaton-Lambert) syndrome - extreme sensitivity; markedly reduced doses needed
Electrolyte disturbance, dehydration, neuromuscular disease, conditions altering block (hypothermia, acid-base disorders)
monitor: Degree of neuromuscular block (train-of-four), ventilation and oxygenation
Heart rate and blood pressure (vagolytic/sympathetic effects)
Recovery of spontaneous breathing and adequacy of reversal before extubation

preg: Pancuronium is a quaternary ammonium compound that crosses the placenta only to a limited extent. There are limited controlled data; it should be used in pregnancy only if clearly needed. It has been used for cesarean delivery and other obstetric surgery by anesthesia specialists who account for possible neonatal effects and ensure neonatal resuscitation capability.
lact: Information on excretion in breast milk is limited. As a quaternary compound it is poorly absorbed orally, so single perioperative use is not expected to result in clinically significant exposure to a breastfed infant. Breastfeeding may generally resume once the mother has recovered from anesthesia.
renal: A substantial proportion of pancuronium is eliminated unchanged by the kidneys (and partly as the 3-hydroxy metabolite). In renal impairment, clearance is reduced and neuromuscular block is prolonged and may accumulate with repeated dosing - reduce doses and monitor block closely; consider an alternative agent in severe renal failure.
hepatic: In hepatic or biliary tract disease, onset may be delayed (larger volume of distribution) and recovery prolonged due to reduced clearance and biliary excretion of the drug and its active metabolite. Titrate carefully with neuromuscular monitoring.

major: Aminoglycoside, polymyxin, and certain other antibiotics - potentiate and prolong neuromuscular block
Inhalational anesthetics (e.g., isoflurane, sevoflurane, enflurane) - enhance and prolong block
Suxamethonium (succinylcholine) given before pancuronium - may enhance/prolong subsequent block
moderate: Other neuromuscular blockers, local anesthetics, antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide), calcium-channel blockers - potentiate block
Diuretics and conditions causing hypokalemia/hypocalcemia/hypermagnesemia - enhance block
minor: Corticosteroids with prolonged neuromuscular blocker use - risk of myopathy/prolonged weakness (especially in ICU)
Chronic anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine) - may shorten duration / cause resistance
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor with peripheral nerve stimulator; correct electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities that alter block.

common: Tachycardia and increase in heart rate (vagolytic effect)
Rise in arterial blood pressure and cardiac output
serious: Prolonged neuromuscular block / residual paralysis and apnea
Prolonged weakness/myopathy with prolonged ICU use, especially with corticosteroids
rare: Histamine release / flushing (less than with benzylisoquinolinium agents)
emergency: Inability to ventilate / respiratory paralysis without ventilatory support
Malignant-hyperthermia-like crisis when combined with triggering anesthetics (rare)

monitoring: Continuous monitoring with a peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four) to titrate dosing and confirm recovery
Controlled mechanical ventilation with oxygenation/capnography throughout the period of paralysis
Heart rate, blood pressure, and ECG (vagolytic and sympathetic effects)
Adequacy of sedation/analgesia to prevent awareness during paralysis
Confirm full reversal and adequate spontaneous ventilation before extubation
counsel: This medicine is given during anesthesia to relax and temporarily paralyze your muscles so the breathing tube can be placed and surgery performed; a machine will breathe for you
It does not put you to sleep or relieve pain - your anesthesia team gives separate medicines for sleep and pain
You will be closely monitored and the effect reversed at the end so your own breathing returns
Tell your anesthesia team about muscle diseases (e.g., myasthenia gravis), kidney or liver problems, and any drug allergies or past anesthesia reactions
Mild muscle aching or a fast heartbeat may occur and is temporary
pk: Onset within ~2-3 minutes; good intubating conditions by ~3-5 minutes
Maximum block within a few minutes of an IV dose
Elimination half-life approximately 2 hours (prolonged in renal/hepatic impairment)
Clinical relaxation ~60-100 minutes from an intubating dose (long-acting)
Refrigerate at 2-8 C; may be stored at room temperature for limited periods per label; do not freeze
pearls: PARALYSIS ONLY - pancuronium provides no sedation, analgesia, or amnesia; always co-administer adequate anesthesia/sedation and analgesia and ALWAYS support ventilation
Long-acting aminosteroid blocker; vagolytic and mild sympathomimetic effects typically cause tachycardia and a rise in blood pressure
Significant renal elimination - block is prolonged and may accumulate in renal failure; titrate down and monitor with a nerve stimulator
Reverse with neostigmine plus an antimuscarinic when recovery has begun, or with sugammadex where available; confirm full reversal before extubation
Greatly enhanced by aminoglycosides, magnesium, volatile anesthetics, hypokalemia and hypothermia; markedly potentiated and contraindicated-level caution in myasthenia gravis
missed: Not applicable - pancuronium is administered as titrated intravenous doses by anesthesia/critical care staff during a procedure or controlled ventilation, not on a patient-managed schedule.
overdose: Overdose produces excessive and prolonged neuromuscular blockade, with respiratory paralysis and apnea. The primary management is to maintain a patent airway and continue controlled mechanical ventilation with adequate sedation until spontaneous recovery occurs. Once recovery begins, neuromuscular block can be antagonized with an anticholinesterase agent (e.g., neostigmine) plus an antimuscarinic (atropine/glycopyrrolate); sugammadex may be used to encapsulate and reverse the block where available. Support cardiovascular status as needed.
